newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar safe-haven status under attack.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar safe-haven status under attack.

text.p: The Singapore dollar, traditionally considered a safe haven during Southeast Asian currency volatility, came under attack on Thursday from U.S. funds, dealers said.
"People think the Singapore dollar would not be attacked because of its safe-haven reputation. But these U.S. funds are testing this reputation," a dealer with a European bank told Reuters.
"All the Americans want to do is to test the various stops to see how low the Sing dollar would go. They want to see how the weak shorts will be triggered out," he said.

At 0429 GMT, the Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4317/27 to the dollar. It had held fairly steady at around 1.43 on Wednesday despite strong pressure on several regional currencies triggered by the de facto devaluation of the Thai baht.
Dealers said the greenback rose against the Singapore dollar after a British party emerged to buy on behalf of some U.S. funds from 1.4310 onwards.
"The Americans were buying the dollar against the Sing since late New York last night and they are just continuing to test all the stops," a dealer with a U.S. bank said.
He said the first stop at 1.4320 was tested and triggered and now U.S. funds were looking to test the next resistance at 1.4330 and 1.4340.

Some dealers said the Singapore currency's "safe-haven" reputation was fairly vulnerable this time due to a weak stock market and an economy whose growth had slowed. "Previously, the Singapore dollar, with the strong economy, was seen as a good buy every time something bad happens in the region. It's not so now. I would tend to be neutral on the Singapore dollar," said the dealer with the European bank.
Most other regional currencies were battered on Wednesday after Thailand announced a managed float exchange rate system, where the baht value would be determined by market forces.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Singapore's de facto central bank, does intervene in the open market but it usually does not comment on its position, said dealers.
MAS officials were not immediately available for comment.
In its annual report issued earlier this week, MAS said it expected the Singapore dollar's modest rate of appreciation to continue.
